Against Civilization: The Case for Radical Rewilding

A Persuasive Essay in the Anarcho-Primitivist Tradition

Introduction

The dominant assumption of modern life is that civilization represents progress — that the trajectory from foraging bands to agricultural settlements to industrial megacities constitutes humanity's ascent toward something better. This essay argues that assumption is precisely backward, that industrial civilization is not humanity's greatest achievement but its most catastrophic mistake, and that genuine human flourishing and ecological survival require not reform, regulation, or technological innovation, but the complete dismantling of industrial systems and a return to the foraging lifeways our species practiced for roughly 95% of its existence.

This is not a nostalgic fantasy. It is a serious argument grounded in anthropology, ecology, evolutionary biology, and political philosophy, drawing on thinkers including John Zerzan, Derrick Jensen, Paul Shepard, Marshall Sahlins, and the broader tradition of anarcho-primitivist and deep ecological thought.

Part One: The Foundational Lie of Progress

Civilization Is Not Natural Human Existence

Homo sapiens emerged approximately 300,000 years ago. Agriculture appeared roughly 10,000 years ago. Industrial civilization is barely 250 years old. By any honest accounting, the foraging band — typically 20 to 50 individuals living in intimate relationship with a specific landscape, practicing sophisticated ecological knowledge accumulated over generations — represents the genuine human baseline. Everything since is the experiment, and the results of that experiment are now visible.

The standard counter-narrative holds that pre-agricultural life was, in Thomas Hobbes's memorable phrase, "solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short." This is mythology serving power, not evidence-based history. Anthropological research has systematically dismantled it.

Marshall Sahlins, in his landmark work Stone Age Economics, demonstrated that hunter-gatherers typically worked 15 to 20 hours per week to meet their material needs. The remainder of their time was devoted to sleep, social interaction, ceremony, play, and contemplative engagement with the living world. Sahlins called them the "original affluent society" — not because they possessed much, but because their wants were calibrated to what their world could genuinely provide. Compare this to the modern industrial worker averaging 47 or more hours per week in labor alienated from any meaningful ecological relationship, spending additional hours in commutes, domestic labor enabled by the expectation of paid work, and the psychological exhaustion that attends constant economic precarity.

The claim that primitive life was brutish requires selective attention to evidence. Skeletal analysis of pre-agricultural populations consistently shows lower rates of nutritional deficiency, less evidence of chronic disease, greater average physical robustness, and less structural violence than populations following the adoption of agriculture. The archaeological and anthropological record suggests that the adoption of agriculture in most regions was not a voluntary improvement but a response to population pressure, climate change, or resource depletion — often imposed through the expansion of already-agricultural neighbors. People did not freely choose the plow. In many cases, they were compelled toward it.

What Agriculture Actually Is

Agriculture is not simply a more efficient way to eat. It is a fundamentally different relationship with the living world — one of domination rather than participation. The farmer does not live within an ecosystem; the farmer replaces an ecosystem. Diverse, multi-layered communities of thousands of species are converted into simplified monocultures serving human nutritional demands. Soil organisms accumulated over millennia are depleted. Water systems are redirected. Wild animals are excluded, poisoned, or hunted to local extinction. Other human beings who refuse participation are driven away or incorporated by force.

Derrick Jensen argues compellingly that civilization is, at its structural core, a system premised on the conversion of living communities into resources. It cannot function otherwise. The civilized logic applied to a forest produces timber. Applied to a river, it produces irrigation. Applied to wild animals, it produces livestock or simply extinction. Applied to human beings who decline participation, it produces slaves, serfs, conscripted soldiers, or colonial subjects. This is not incidental to civilization. It is the logic civilization runs on.

The myth of agricultural abundance conceals a more disturbing reality: agriculture feeds more people than foraging, but it feeds them more poorly, more precariously, and at catastrophic cost to the systems that actually sustain life. The great famines of history — the Irish Famine, the Bengal Famines, the Soviet famines — were not failures of agriculture but products of it: monoculture's vulnerability to disease and climate variation, combined with political economies that extract food from the hungry to feed the powerful. Foraging societies, by contrast, were resilient precisely because they participated in diverse ecosystems that provided varied nutritional resources. Their "inefficiency" was actually distributed risk management of the highest sophistication.

Part Two: Industrial Civilization as Omnicidal System

The Scale of Ongoing Destruction

Let us be clear about what industrial civilization is currently doing to the living world.

We are in the midst of the sixth mass extinction event in Earth's 4.5-billion-year history — and the first caused by a single species. Current extinction rates are estimated at 100 to 1,000 times the background extinction rate. Vertebrate populations have declined by an average of 69% since 1970, according to the World Wildlife Fund's Living Planet Report. Insect biomass in heavily studied regions has declined by 75% or more over the same period. Roughly half of the world's topsoil has been lost to agricultural erosion since 1960. Freshwater systems are collapsing globally. Oceanic oxygen-minimum zones are expanding. And over all of this looms the accelerating destabilization of the atmospheric chemistry that made complex life on Earth possible in the first place.

No honest engagement with these facts permits the conclusion that industrial civilization is compatible with the continuation of the living systems it depends on. The civilization is consuming its own foundations. It is eating the world.

Technological optimists insist that better technology will solve the problems created by technology. Solar panels will replace fossil fuels. Vertical farms will restore land to nature. Carbon capture machines will clean the atmosphere. Genetic engineering will resurrect species. This argument has been made continuously throughout the industrial period, and throughout that period the ecological situation has continuously worsened. The most technologically advanced period in human history is simultaneously the most ecologically destructive period. The correlation is not coincidental; it is causal.

Technology does not simply replace previous systems with cleaner alternatives. It expands total throughput. When steam engines improved efficiency, coal consumption increased rather than decreased — what economists call the Jevons Paradox. When agricultural technology increased crop yields, more land was brought under cultivation rather than less. When communication technology enabled remote work, workers moved farther from employment centers rather than eliminating commutes. Efficiency improvements under capitalism reliably enable expansion rather than reduction. There is no reason to expect this pattern to change. The only intervention that actually reduces ecological impact is reducing the scale of the system itself.

What Civilization Does to Human Beings

Industrial civilization is not merely ecologically catastrophic. It is psychologically and spiritually devastating.

The psychiatric burden of modern life is staggering. In wealthy, industrialized nations — the supposed beneficiaries of technological progress — rates of depression, anxiety, addiction, loneliness, and suicide have risen consistently alongside material prosperity. The United States, the world's wealthiest nation by most measures, leads the developed world in opioid addiction, mass incarceration, military violence, and political despair. The World Health Organization identifies depression as a leading cause of global disability. These are not marginal problems awaiting better pharmaceutical management. They are structural products of a way of life systematically incompatible with human psychological needs.

Paul Shepard, the ecologist and philosopher, argued in works including Nature and Madness that civilization produces a pervasive developmental pathology. Human beings evolved as participants in complex, multi-species communities. Our nervous systems, our perceptual capacities, our emotional lives, our sense of meaning were shaped by 300,000 years of intimate daily relationship with specific landscapes and the animals, plants, fungi, and waters within them. Industrial civilization systematically strips those relationships away, replacing them with mediated, transactional interactions with other psychologically damaged humans in environments designed for economic productivity rather than creaturely flourishing. Shepard's argument is not metaphorical. The ecological impoverishment of modern environments is a literal developmental impoverishment. Children growing up without sustained contact with wild, non-human life are growing up with stunted human development.

The alienation that Marx identified as capitalism's signature pathology goes deeper than economic relations. It is, at root, ecological alienation: the severance of human beings from the living communities to which they belong. No adjustment of property relations resolves it as long as civilization continues replacing those communities with human-dominated monocultures. A socialist industrial civilization is still an industrial civilization. It still runs on the same foundational logic of converting living systems into resources. The alienation follows from that logic, not from who controls the means of production.

Part Three: The Case for Dismantling

Why Reform Cannot Work

Every serious environmental movement of the past half-century has operated on a reform model: pressure governments to regulate the worst excesses of industrial production, develop cleaner technologies, establish protected areas, shift consumer behavior. The cumulative result of fifty years of serious, committed environmental activism within these parameters is an ecological situation dramatically worse than when that activism began.

This is not a failure of effort or intelligence. It is a structural failure. Industrial civilization generates political power proportional to economic scale. The largest corporations and most ecologically destructive industries are therefore the most politically powerful actors in every society organized around industrial production. They consistently capture regulatory agencies, fund political parties, shape public discourse, and neutralize threats to their operation. The regulatory victories of environmentalism — the Clean Air Act, the Endangered Species Act, emissions trading schemes, protected area networks — are real, and without them things would be worse, but they are systematically insufficient. They establish limits that are consistently pushed against, weakened, and rolled back. They accept the fundamental legitimacy of the system they attempt to constrain.

More fundamentally, reform efforts accept the premise that industrial civilization can be made compatible with ecological health. The evidence of the past century suggests this premise is false. A civilization premised on continuous economic growth on a finite planet with finite ecological systems cannot be reformed into ecological sustainability. It can only be transformed — which is to say, it must cease to be what it is.

What Dismantling Means

The call to dismantle industrial civilization does not mean a sudden, violent collapse — though it is worth noting that a sudden, violent collapse is what industrial civilization is currently engineering for itself through ecological destabilization, and that the civilized response to that trajectory is simply to continue. It means a deliberate, committed project of withdrawal from industrial systems and the reconstruction of human communities organized around ecological participation rather than ecological extraction.

In practical terms, this begins with rewilding: allowing agricultural and industrial lands to return to diverse, self-organizing ecological communities. It means learning, recovering, and practicing the skills of ecological participation — plant knowledge, animal tracking, fire tending, water reading, the thousand forms of practical intelligence that constitute genuine ecological competence. It means rebuilding human communities at scales and densities compatible with foraging — not as an immediate universal prescription but as a long-term trajectory and present aspiration. It means refusing, wherever possible, participation in industrial systems: not as individual consumer choice (which changes nothing structurally) but as community withdrawal, mutual aid, and the construction of genuinely alternative ways of living.

The population objection arises immediately: eight billion people cannot live as foragers. This is true, and it confronts us with an uncomfortable conclusion that must be stated plainly rather than evaded. Industrial civilization has produced a human population that industrial civilization is now failing to sustainably support. A world returned to ecological balance would support a dramatically smaller human population — estimates vary, but figures in the range of tens of millions to a few hundred million are commonly cited in the primitivist literature, compared to the Earth's carrying capacity under a foraging regime. The question is not whether population will decline — the ecological trajectory makes some form of population decline essentially certain — but whether that decline happens through the catastrophic collapse of industrial civilization's own making, or through a more intentional, humane transition.

This is the most difficult and most important part of the argument. It requires holding simultaneously the recognition that industrial civilization is already producing the conditions for massive human suffering and death through ecological collapse, and the genuine moral seriousness about human life that might seem to argue for maintaining industrial systems that currently feed large numbers of people. The honest primitivist response is that industrial systems are not actually on a trajectory to continue feeding those people. The question is what path leads to less overall suffering — continuation of a system accelerating toward catastrophic collapse, or deliberate transition toward something with a genuine long-term future.

What Is Lost and What Is Gained

The primitivist argument does not deny that dismantling industrial civilization involves losses. Many of them are real. Modern medicine has relieved enormous suffering for those who can access it. Certain forms of communication and creative expression enabled by digital technology are genuinely valuable. Scientific knowledge accumulated through industrial-period research is real knowledge, even if much of it has been applied destructively.

But the calculus is not simply what civilization has produced against what it has destroyed. It is whether what civilization has produced is compatible with the continuation of the living systems on which everything depends. And it is whether the forms of meaning, connection, and joy that civilization enables are superior to those available in genuinely ecological human communities.

On both counts, the evidence argues against civilization. The medicines that extend individual lives cannot compensate for the destruction of the atmospheric, hydrological, and biological systems that make life possible. The creative expressions enabled by digital technology cannot substitute for the forms of meaning — ceremony, story, ecological knowledge, multi-generational community, intimate relationship with specific places and their creatures — that industrial civilization systematically destroys.

What the foraging life offers, at its best — and acknowledging that no human community, foraging or otherwise, is without conflict and suffering — is genuine participation in a living world rather than estrangement from it. It offers communities scaled to human psychological capacity rather than to economic efficiency. It offers work that is meaningful because it is ecologically embedded rather than alienated and abstract. It offers a human life that is genuinely a part of the web of life rather than at war with it.

Conclusion: The Only Honest Position

Industrial civilization is killing the living world. It is doing so not through specific bad decisions that better regulation could address, but through its foundational logic of converting ecological communities into resources for human consumption. It is simultaneously producing the conditions for its own collapse and for the collapse of the living systems it depends upon.

The comfortable positions — green capitalism, sustainable development, ecological modernism — ask us to believe that the system causing the catastrophe can, with sufficient political will and technological ingenuity, be redirected to prevent it. Fifty years of serious effort in those directions, during which the ecological situation has consistently worsened, is not encouraging evidence.

The primitivist position asks something harder: genuine reckoning with the possibility that the experiment of civilization has failed, and that human survival and ecological restoration require not its improvement but its end. This is not a position of despair. The foraging life, the life our species lived successfully for 95% of its existence, was not a life of deprivation. By most anthropological measures it was a life of genuine richness — ecologically, socially, psychologically. We have not evolved beyond it. We have been removed from it. We can, over time and with genuine commitment, return.

The living world is attempting to recover from what civilization has done to it. Every piece of land that is rewilded, every industrial system that is abandoned, every human community that rebuilds genuine ecological competence is a contribution to that recovery. The question for each person living within industrial civilization is not whether this argument is comfortable or convenient, but whether it is true.

The evidence suggests that it is.

This essay presents the strongest available version of anarcho-primitivist and deep ecological arguments. Readers should engage these ideas critically, including examining the contested empirical claims, the serious ethical questions about population, the romanticization risks in primitivist thought, and the counterarguments from thinkers including Steven Pinker, Ruth DeFries, Stewart Brand, and others who dispute central premises of this tradition.

Title: The Imperative of Collapse: Reclaiming Ecological Harmony and Human Authenticity Through the Dismantling of Industrial Civilization

Introduction
Industrial civilization, with its sprawling cities, digital networks, and mechanized exploitation of nature, stands as a monument to human ingenuity—and a harbinger of ecological and spiritual ruin. The relentless pursuit of progress has severed humanity’s intrinsic bond with the Earth, plunging us into a vortex of climate collapse, biodiversity extinction, and existential alienation. To restore balance to the planet and reclaim our authentic existence as embedded members of the biosphere, we must confront an uncomfortable truth: industrial civilization and its technological appendages are irredeemable. Only through their complete dismantling, and a radical reversion to pre-agricultural, hunter-gatherer lifeways, can we hope to heal the Earth and ourselves.

I. Industrial Civilization: A System of Systemic Ecocide

The ecological case against industrial society is irrefutable. Since the Industrial Revolution, atmospheric CO₂ levels have surged by 50%, driving catastrophic warming, superstorms, and sea-level rise. Deforestation for agriculture and urbanization has erased half of Earth’s forests, while industrial agriculture—dependent on synthetic fertilizers, monocropping, and pesticides—has degraded 75% of global soil. Oceans, acidified by carbon absorption and littered with plastic, face a collapse of marine food webs, with studies warning of fishless seas by 2050.

This is not a malfunction but a feature of industrial capitalism: a system predicated on infinite growth in a finite world. Renewable energy and “green technology” are illusions of decoupling; they still demand lithium mines, rare-earth minerals, and vast infrastructures that ravage ecosystems. Even a “sustainable” industrial model requires domination over nature, reducing rivers to hydropower, forests to carbon sinks, and animals to data points. To tinker at the margins—electric cars, solar panels—is to ignore the elephant in the room: the entire system must go.

II. Pre-Agricultural Lifeways: Models of Sustainability and Resilience

Before the rise of agriculture 10,000 years ago, humans thrived for millennia as nomadic hunter-gatherers, living lightly on the land. Anthropological studies of remaining indigenous communities, such as the Hadza of Tanzania or the San of southern Africa, reveal societies with negligible ecological footprints. They practiced “fire-stick farming” to enhance biodiversity, hunted only what was needed, and moved seasonally to allow ecosystems to regenerate. Far from “primitive,” these lifeways were sophisticated adaptations to place, embodying what philosopher John Zerzan calls “the original affluent society”—a state where minimal labor provided abundance, leaving time for art, storytelling, and community.

Critics romanticize industrial “progress” as a liberation from scarcity, yet pre-agricultural societies enjoyed richer diets, fewer diseases, and more leisure. Agriculture birthed hierarchy, slavery, and famine; industrialization amplified these inequities into global capitalism’s death grip. To dismantle modernity is not to regress, but to evolve toward a decentralized, low-impact existence aligned with ecological limits.

III. The Alienation of Modernity: A Crisis of Being

Industrial civilization does not merely destroy ecosystems—it fractures the human psyche. Trapped in cubicles, scrolling through screens, or competing in the gig economy, modern humans suffer an epidemic of depression, anxiety, and loneliness. Social bonds have withered under individualism and consumerism; suicide rates have risen 35% since 1999. Even our bodies rebel: sedentary lifestyles spawn chronic illness, while processed foods fuel obesity and diabetes.

Hunter-gatherers, conversely, lived immersed in sensory-rich environments, their days shaped by the rhythms of sunrise, migration, and moon cycles. Their labor was meaningful—crafting tools, foraging, sharing stories around fires—and their communities egalitarian, with resources distributed communally. This is not mere nostalgia; it is a blueprint for reconnecting with our biological and social instincts. Technology, from smartphones to surveillance states, has become a prosthetic for our disconnection, mediating every experience. To shed it is to reclaim our humanity.

IV. Rebutting the Cult of Progress

Skeptics argue that modern medicine, transportation, and communication justify industrial systems. But these benefits are both ecocidal and inequitable: one-third of humanity lacks clean water while the Global North hoards resources. Antibiotics, born of industrial labs, are rendered useless by overuse; meanwhile, traditional herbal medicine, attuned to local ecologies, offers sustainable healing.

Others fear chaos in collapse, yet industrial society is already unraveling—wars over resources, antibiotic-resistant pathogens, grid failures. A managed descent into decentralized, land-based communities could mitigate this, prioritizing local resilience over global fragility. The Amish, who reject industrialization for intentional simplicity, demonstrate that such transitions are viable.

Conclusion: A Pact with the Earth

The choice is stark: persist on our current path toward a scorched, depopulated planet, or embrace a future rooted in humility and reciprocity. Dismantling industrial civilization does not mean destroying all tools, but rejecting the ideology of domination. Windmills and stone axes alike are moral in context; what matters is the relationship they foster—exploitation or symbiosis.

To return to pre-agricultural wisdom is not to abandon innovation, but to redefine it as stewardship. Imagine a world where rivers run free, children learn the names of plants, and communities celebrate the return of salmon and songbirds. This is not a utopia—it is a contract with reality. The Earth does not need humans to “save” her; she needs us to stop waging war against her. The hour is late, but the path is clear. Collapse industrial civilization. Reclaim your birthright as a creature of the forest, the tundra, the Earth. Survive.

Core Critiques of Modern Civilization

Anti-civilization theorists view modernity as a regime of alienation and ecological collapse, claiming that small-scale, wild societies offer a path to reclaim autonomy and heal the planet. Critics, however, argue that their vision is impractical and nostalgic, ignoring the complexity of human history and the ethical challenges of dismantling civilization. Title: The Imperative of Dismantling Industrial Civilization: A Return to Primitive, Pre-Agricultural Lifeways

Introduction

The escalating ecological crisis, coupled with the alienation of humans from nature and each other, signals the urgency to reassess and radically transform our current mode of existence. Industrial civilization and its attendant technological systems, built on the presumption of endless growth and exploitation, have precipitated ecological devastation, social inequities, and spiritual impoverishment. This essay argues for the complete dismantling of industrial civilization and advocates a return to primitive, pre-agricultural lifeways as an essential step towards restoring ecological balance and fostering authentic human existence.

The Ecological Imperative

Industrial civilization, with its dependence on fossil fuels, deforestation, and intensive agriculture, has pushed the Earth's ecosystems to the brink of collapse. Climate change, biodiversity loss, soil depletion, and ocean acidification are not isolated issues but interconnected symptoms of a system fundamentally at odds with ecological harmony (McKibben, 2010). The imperative to dismantle this system arises from the necessity to halt and reverse these trends, preserving the planet's capacity to support complex life forms, including humans.

Pre-agricultural societies, often nomadic or semi-nomadic, maintained a sustainable equilibrium with their environments. Their low population densities, minimal resource extraction, and intimate knowledge of local ecosystems enabled them to live within the Earth's carrying capacity (Sahlins, 1972). A return to such lifeways would dramatically reduce human environmental impact, allowing for ecological restoration and the reestablishment of biodiversity.

The Social Imperative

Industrial civilization, despite its promises of prosperity, has engendered vast social inequities. Wealth disparities, labor exploitation, and systemic injustices are inherent to a system that concentrates power and resources in the hands of a privileged few (Picketty, 2014). Moreover, the atomization and alienation fostered by modern societies have led to epidemics of mental health crises, loneliness, and social fragmentation.

In contrast, pre-agricultural societies were typically egalitarian, with shared resources and collective decision-making processes (Boehm, 1999). Their smaller, kinship-based communities fostered strong social bonds, mutual aid, and a sense of belonging. By returning to these social structures, we can address the root causes of many contemporary social ills, nurturing healthier, more cohesive, and equitable communities.

The Existential Imperative

Industrial civilization, with its emphasis on productivity, consumption, and technological mediation, has alienated humans from the natural world and their own essence. Modern lifestyles, divorced from the rhythms and processes of nature, have led to a profound sense of disconnection and existential malaise.

Primitive lifeways, grounded in a deep connection to the natural world, offer a path to authentic human existence. Living in intimate relationship with the land, its inhabitants, and one's community fosters a sense of belonging, purpose, and spiritual wholeness (Abram, 1996). This existential shift is not merely about romanticizing the past but about reclaiming our fundamental humanity and restoring our place within the web of life.

Addressing Objections

Critics may argue that such a radical transition is neither feasible nor desirable, citing the advantages of modern medicine, technology, and urban living. However, the viability of pre-agricultural lifeways has been demonstrated by their sustained existence over millennia and their continued practice by some indigenous communities today. Furthermore, the accelerating collapse of ecosystems and the increasing instability of industrial societies suggest that the real utopianism lies in believing that the current system can persist indefinitely.

Rather than a wholesale rejection of all technology, a return to primitive lifeways entails a critical reassessment of which tools and practices are truly beneficial and compatible with ecological and social well-being. This approach acknowledges that some technologies may be retained or reinvented, but always in service to a fundamentally different set of values and objectives.

Conclusion

The dismantling of industrial civilization and a return to primitive, pre-agricultural lifeways is not a call for privation or austerity but an invitation to abundance, connection, and meaning. It is a recognition that the story of endless growth and domination has reached its terminus, and that a new, older story of interdependence and harmony is waiting to be reclaimed. This transition is not merely about survival but about flourishing—about creating a world where humans can live with dignity, in harmony with each other and the living Earth.

In the face of ecological catastrophe, social inequities, and existential alienation, we must muster the courage to envision and enact a radically different way of being. The future of life on Earth, including our own, depends on it.

  • Abram, D. (1996). The Spell of the Sensuous: Perception and Language in a More-Than-Human World. Vintage.
  • Boehm, C. (1999). Hierarchy in the Forest: The Evolution of Egalitarian Behavior. Harvard University Press.
  • McKibben, B. (2010). Eaarth: Making a Life on a Tough New Planet. Times Books.
  • Picketty, T. (2014). Capital in the Twenty-First Century. Harvard University Press.
  • Sahlins, M. (1972). Stone Age Economics. AldineTransaction.

A central argument of anti-civilization thinkers (most notably John Zerzan) is that civilization creates deep psychological alienation.

  • Reconnection with Nature: In modern society, humans view themselves as separate from—and superior to—the natural world. This dualism causes existential emptiness. Reverting to hunter-gatherer life dissolves this barrier, reintegrating humanity into the "web of life."
  • Symbolic vs. Direct Experience: Primitivists argue that language, mathematics, and technology act as symbolic mediators between us and reality. We experience the world through screens and words rather than through direct sensory experience. Abolishing technology allows for a return to immediate, unmediated consciousness.
  • Mental Illness: Proponents point to studies of remaining hunter-gatherer societies that show remarkably low rates of depression, anxiety, and chronic stress compared to modern populations. They attribute this to the lack of social hierarchy, the pace of life, and the physicality of existence.

2. The End of Domination and Hierarchy

This perspective posits that hierarchy and oppression are built into the very DNA of civilization.

  • Division of Labor: Civilization requires specialization (farmers, soldiers, factory workers). This makes people interdependent but also controllable. If you do not know how to grow food or build shelter, you must obey those who do. Hunter-gatherer societies are generally characterized by egalitarianism and a lack of division of labor; everyone possesses the skills necessary for survival.
  • Surplus and Power: Agriculture created surplus food, which allowed for storage. Surplus required managers, guards, and eventually rulers. By returning to immediate-return subsistence (hunting and gathering what is needed now), the material basis for hoarding wealth and establishing power structures vanishes.
  • Domestication: The ideology views domestication—of animals, plants, and eventually humans—as a process of enslavement. Just as a cow is enslaved by a farmer, the human is enslaved by the system they built.

3. Ecological Sustainability

This is perhaps the most practical argument: technological civilization is inherently unsustainable.

  • The Energy Trap: Industrial civilization relies on non-renewable resources (fossil fuels) and the destruction of the biosphere. No amount of "green technology" can sustain 8 billion people without continuing the extraction of resources.
  • Carrying Capacity: Primitive lifestyles have a much lower impact per capita. Living within the immediate carrying capacity of the land is viewed as the only truly ecological way of living, whereas modern "environmentalism" is seen as merely managing the rate of collapse.

4. Reclamation of Autonomy

Modern technology is often criticized for making humans dependent on complex systems they cannot understand or repair.

  • Technological Dependency: If the power grid fails or supply chains break, the modern human is helpless. The primitive human is autonomous, possessing all necessary knowledge for survival.
  • The "Leisure" Society: Anthropological studies often suggest that hunter-gatherers spent significantly less time working for survival (obtaining food and shelter) than modern wage-slaves spend in offices or factories. The argument is that abandoning technology frees up time for socializing, art, play, and spiritual exploration.

5. Community and Social Cohesion

In a state of nature, humans lived in small, tight-knit bands (Dunbar’s number suggests we are cognitively wired for about 150 relationships).

  • Shared Fate: In a primitive band, the survival of the individual depends on the cooperation of the group. This fosters deep empathy and solidarity, contrasting with the hyper-individualism and isolation of the modern metropolis.

To the anti-civilization ideologue, dismantling technology is not an act of self-destruction, but an act of healing. They believe that while we might lose modern medicine and convenience, we would regain our freedom, our sanity, our community, and our place within the natural order.

The Great Unwinding: Why Industrial Civilization Must Fall

A Persuasive Case for De-Civilization and the Return to the Wild

Introduction: The Lie of Progress

We stand at a precipice, though most of us have been so thoroughly conditioned by the very systems destroying us that we cannot perceive it. The story of civilization—that we are ascending toward something greater, that each generation is better than the last—is perhaps the most successful myth ever propagated. It is a myth maintained not by truth, but by habit, inertia, and the material addiction of billions of humans to technologies that have simultaneously extended their reach and truncated their existence.

The thesis I will defend is not a comfortable one, but it is, I argue, the only honest reckoning with the evidence: industrial civilization is a death cult wearing the mask of prosperity. The only viable path forward—a path that offers any chance at ecological restoration, genuine human fulfillment, and the continuation of life on Earth beyond the next several centuries—is the deliberate, organized dismantling of industrial technological systems and a return to small-scale, land-based, pre-agricultural lifeways.

This is not nostalgia. It is not romanticism. It is a structural argument, grounded in ecology, anthropology, psychology, and the plain arithmetic of thermodynamics.

I. The Ecological Accounting: Collapse Is Not a Possibility, It Is a Trajectory

Let us begin with what is no longer disputable among serious scientists, even if the conclusions remain unspoken in polite policy circles.

The biosphere is dying. Not in some slow, reversible way, but in cascading, self-reinforcing ways that increasingly resemble the mathematical signature of collapse. The Holocene—the stable climatic period that allowed the last ten thousand years of agriculture, cities, and civilization—was a narrow window. We have blown it open.

Consider the ledger:

  • Climate: The concentration of CO₂ in the atmosphere now exceeds 420 parts per million, a level not seen in at least 800,000 years, and likely not in 14 million years. The consequences are already manifesting in extreme weather, destabilized food systems, and compounding feedbacks—permafrost thaw, ice sheet disintegration, ocean acidification—that threaten to push the system beyond any human capacity to manage.

  • Biodiversity: We are in the midst of what biologists call the Sixth Mass Extinction. Species are vanishing at a rate 1,000 to 10,000 times the background rate. Insect biomass has declined by over 75% in some regions within a single generation. The living fabric of the planet—evolved over billions of years—is unraveling in a matter of decades.

  • Soil and Water: Topsoil loss is rendering vast tracts of agricultural land infertile. Aquifers that took millennia to fill are being drained in years. Rivers that once sustained civilizations run dry or toxic. The water cycle itself is destabilizing.

  • Pollution: Microplastics have infiltrated the deepest ocean trenches and the human bloodstream. PFAS "forever chemicals" contaminate virtually every ecosystem on Earth. We have produced so many synthetic substances that the geological record will bear a clear chemical marker—a distinct stratum of plastic and radionuclides that future geologists (if any exist) will call the Anthropocene layer: a monument to our toxicity.

The liberal response to this catastrophe has been consistent for forty years: more technology, more efficiency, more policy, more "green growth." And every year, despite the proliferation of solar panels and electric vehicles and carbon credits, the total ecological footprint of civilization increases. Global CO₂ emissions continue to rise. Deforestation accelerates. The aggregate mass of human industrial activity—what researchers call "technomass"—has now exceeded the total mass of all living organisms on Earth. We are literally converting the biosphere into infrastructure, and then celebrating when we make the infrastructure slightly less destructive.

This is not a system that can be reformed. The mathematics do not permit it. There is no amount of "efficiency" that can offset the Jevons paradox—the observation that as technology makes resource use more efficient, consumption increases, negating the gains. There is no renewable energy source that can power industrial civilization at current scale without its own devastating ecological footprint—mining lithium, cobalt, and rare earths, destroying landscapes for solar farms, building wind turbines from materials that cannot be recycled.

The fundamental problem is not fossil fuels. The fundamental problem is civilization itself—the scale, the complexity, the extraction, the demand. Fossil fuels were simply the accelerant that allowed a system already destructive in principle to become destructive at planetary scale. Remove fossil fuels and keep the system, and the system will simply find other means of destruction, as it always has.

The only mathematically honest conclusion is that industrial civilization must be reduced to a scale compatible with the biosphere's regenerative capacity. And that scale is far below what we currently inhabit.

II. The Anthropological Record: Thirty-Thousand Years of Evidence

We need not rely on speculation about what non-civilized life might look like. We have extensive evidence—from the archaeological record, from ethnographic observation of contemporary hunter-gatherer societies, and from the analysis of human physiology and psychology—that pre-agricultural humans lived lives of remarkable sufficiency, health, and ecological integration.

The conventional narrative tells us that agriculture was a great leap forward—that it freed humans from the "hardship" of foraging and permitted the flowering of culture, art, and civilization. This narrative is, to put it bluntly, backwards.

The paleontological record tells a different story. The adoption of agriculture was associated with:

  • A dramatic decline in nutritional diversity and food quality. Early agriculturalists relied on a narrow range of grains, leading to malnutrition, dental disease, and deficiency syndromes. Hunter-gatherers, by contrast, consumed dozens of plant and animal species, achieving nutritional completeness that no monoculture could match.

  • A collapse in average height and skeletal health. The earliest agriculturalists were measurably shorter, more disease-ridden, and more physically degraded than their foraging predecessors. This trend is well-documented in every region where agriculture was independently adopted.

  • A population explosion driven not by improved welfare, but by increased fertility and infant survival at the cost of everything else. Agriculture permitted more births, but those births produced lives of greater labor, greater disease, and shorter duration. It was not liberation; it was a demographic trap.

  • The emergence of hierarchy, warfare, slavery, and patriarchy. Property, surplus, and sedentism created the conditions for accumulation, domination, and organized violence on a scale previously impossible. War, which had existed in some form among foragers, became systemic, totalizing, and genocidal.

Anthropologists like Marshall Sahlins, James C. Scott, and Yasuhisa Miyake have documented that contemporary and historical hunter-gatherer societies consistently exhibit shorter working hours (typically 15–20 hours per week of subsistence labor), greater dietary diversity, more equitable gender relations, more leisure, and lower rates of interpersonal violence than their civilized counterparts.

These are not primitive failures. They are, by every measurable standard of human well-being, superior adaptations. The question is not whether such a way of life is possible—we know it is, because humans lived it successfully for hundreds of thousands of years. The question is whether we have the courage to choose it again.

III. The Psychological and Spiritual Crisis: Civilization as Alienation

Beyond the material accounting of collapse, there is a crisis that is harder to quantify but no less real: civilization has made human beings profoundly, structurally unhappy.

Consider the state of the modern human psyche:

  • Rates of depression, anxiety, and suicidality are at or near all-time highs across the industrialized world, and are now rising rapidly in developing nations as they undergo industrialization.

  • Loneliness is epidemic. In nations that have the most advanced communication technology in history, people report having fewer meaningful relationships than at any point in the anthropological record.

  • Attention spans have collapsed. The capacity for deep, sustained thought—the capacity that produced the very philosophy and science civilization claims to celebrate—is eroding under the relentless assault of algorithmic distraction.

  • A sense of meaninglessness pervades modern life. Surveys consistently show that large percentages of the population find their work unfulfilling, their lives purposeless, their futures bleak. The "affluent" nations report some of the highest rates of existential despair.

  • Children are increasingly neurologically distressed—rising rates of ADHD, autism spectrum conditions, anxiety disorders, and developmental delays correlate with urbanization, screen exposure, loss of unstructured play, and disconnection from the natural world.

These are not incidental features of modern life. They are direct consequences of the civilizational system. The human organism evolved over millions of years in intimate relationship with a specific kind of environment: small kin-based groups, constant physical movement, direct sensory engagement with the natural world, meaningful labor tied to immediate survival, and embeddedness in ecological cycles. Every single one of these conditions has been destroyed or severely degraded by industrial civilization.

We sit in climate-controlled boxes. We stare at illuminated rectangles for 10–12 hours a day. We consume foods that bear no resemblance to what our bodies evolved to process. We labor at tasks so abstract and disconnected from any tangible outcome that the word "bullshit jobs" has entered the lexicon with full sociological legitimacy. We are surrounded by millions of strangers and known by almost no one. We are, in the most literal biological sense, living in environments to which we are radically maladapted.

The psychologist John Calhoun's famous "rat park" experiments—though conducted on rodents—illustrated a principle with disturbing human relevance: when animals are placed in overcrowded, artificial, resource-depleted environments, they develop pathologies—violence, withdrawal, reproductive dysfunction, addiction. When placed in enriched, spacious, naturalistic environments, these pathologies largely vanish. We are not rats, but we are animals, and the principle holds: the environment shapes the organism. And the environment we have built is one of profound deprivation disguised as abundance.

A return to land-based, small-group living is not a retreat into primitivism. It is a return to the actual conditions under which the human psyche thrives. It is, in the deepest sense, a homecoming.

IV. The Objections: Answering the Skeptics

At this point, a cascade of objections naturally arises. I will address the most serious ones.

"What about medicine? What about the cure for cancer?"

This is perhaps the most emotionally potent objection, and it deserves a thoughtful response. It is true that modern biomedicine has achieved remarkable feats. But let us be precise about what it has achieved, and at what cost.

Modern medicine has largely succeeded in two domains: treating acute injuries and infectious diseases. The treatment of chronic lifestyle diseases—heart disease, type 2 diabetes, many cancers—has been far less successful, and these diseases are overwhelmingly products of civilization itself: sedentary living, processed food, environmental toxins, chronic stress. A population living a pre-agricultural lifeway would have vanishingly low rates of these conditions. The "cures" civilization offers are, in large part, treatments for diseases civilization created.

As for infectious disease: the hunter-gatherer lifestyle, with its low population density, high mobility, and constant exposure to diverse microbial environments, offered robust immunological protection. It was agriculture and urbanization—sedentism, animal domestication, crowding, poor sanitation—that created the vast majority of epidemic diseases: smallpox, measles, influenza, bubonic plague. The very diseases for which we celebrate modern medicine are largely consequences of the very civilization we are examining.

I do not argue that a return to foraging would eliminate all suffering or death. But I argue that the net health outcomes—adjusting for what civilization gives and what it takes away—are not clearly inferior, and may be substantially superior.

"Population would have to decrease dramatically."

Yes. This is not a comfortable truth, but it is a true one. The Earth cannot sustain 8 billion humans at any level of industrial activity without catastrophic ecological damage. The only question is whether the decrease happens through deliberate, humane reorganization or through the brutal, chaotic collapse that industrial civilization is already engineering. I argue for the former. A gradual, voluntary transition to land-based living, distributed across the planet, would permit a population decline through reduced fertility (which consistently accompanies such lifeways) rather than through mass starvation, pandemic, and war.

"This is unrealistic. People will never voluntarily give up technology."

This objection mistakes the nature of the argument. I am not arguing that people will voluntarily dismantle civilization in a single generation. I am arguing that civilization will dismantle itself, because it is thermodynamically impossible to sustain. The only choice we have is whether the dismantling is managed—with intention, wisdom, and compassion—or catastrophic—with suffering, chaos, and the near-total loss of both human life and ecological integrity.

The question is not whether we will lose industrial civilization. The question is whether we will do so with our humanity intact.

"This is elitist. You'd deny the poor the benefits of technology."

This objection inverts the actual dynamic. The "benefits" of technology for the global poor have been, overwhelmingly, exploitation: resource extraction, land theft, wage slavery, environmental contamination, and cultural destruction. The poorest people on Earth—the sweatshop workers, the miners, the sweatshop farmers growing export crops while their own children starve—are not beneficiaries of civilization. They are its fuel. What I propose offers them something civilization never has: autonomy, agency, connection to land, and freedom from the machinery of extraction.

V. The Moral Imperative: What Do We Owe the Future?

Let me close with a question that I believe cuts through all the policy debates, all the technological proposals, all the incrementalist fantasies:

What kind of ancestor do we want to be?

If industrial civilization continues on its current trajectory—and all evidence suggests it will, absent radical intervention—the inheritance we leave to future generations (if there are any) will be a planet so degraded that the word "inherited" becomes a cruel joke. We will leave them:

  • A climate system in chaos, with feedbacks locked in that will take millennia to stabilize.
  • A biosphere stripped of its most magnificent and ecologically critical species.
  • Soils too depleted to grow food without industrial inputs.
  • Oceans acidified and depleted.
  • A geological record poisoned with the chemical detritus of our way of life.
  • And a psychic legacy of alienation, despair, and spiritual disconnection so profound that future humans—if they survive—will look back on us with the same mixture of horror and bewilderment with which we look back on the architects of the most destructive empires.

Or we can be the generation that chose differently. That looked at the catastrophe bearing down upon us and had the courage—not the courage of soldiers or revolutionaries, but the far harder courage of letting go. Of stepping down from the altar of progress and returning to the earth. Of trusting that the human species, which thrived for hundreds of thousands of years without electricity, without computers, without the machinery of industrial extraction, can thrive again.

This is not defeat. It is maturity. It is what a truly intelligent species would do when confronted with the empirical evidence that its current trajectory leads to its own annihilation and the destruction of everything it claims to value.

The dismantling of industrial civilization is not a tragedy to be mourned. It is a liberation to be embraced—a liberation from the machine, from the commodity, from the abstract and the alienating, and a return to the concrete, the tactile, the living, and the real.

The question is not whether we can survive without industrial civilization. We already know we can. We did it for most of human history.

The question is whether we have the wisdom to remember what we have forgotten.

The forest does not need us. But we, it turns out, need the forest. We always have.
